ambiguous.why: ISC2 CC treats ransomware as the canonical denial-of-access case, so Availability is the keyed answer. But a student can argue the data has been unauthorisedly transformed (Integrity), and modern double-extortion ransomware exfiltrates first (Confidentiality). The item does not say the data is exfiltrated, which is why Availability wins, but the objection is legitimate.

Immutability is an integrity property — it stops the backup being altered. I key it IN because in a ransomware scenario the purpose of the offline copy is to get records back and reachable, which is availability, and the prompt names ransomware survival explicitly. A student who reads 'immutable' as the operative word and calls it integrity has a defensible reading.

RBAC limits which accounts ransomware can act through, so it contributes to availability indirectly. The prompt says 'primarily protects', and RBAC's primary purpose is confidentiality/least privilege, so OUT stands — but the word 'primarily' is doing all the work.

ambiguous.item: Keeping a tamper-evident audit log of who changed each record
ambiguous.alternative: no in-bucket alternative; some texts call this 'accountability' rather than non-repudiation
ambiguous.why: Several textbooks reserve non-repudiation for cryptographic proof (digital signatures) and file audit logging under accountability or integrity. Given only these three buckets, non-repudiation is the intended answer — 'tamper-evident' plus 'who changed each record' is exactly the evidentiary function — but a student taught the stricter cryptographic definition has a fair objection.

ambiguous.item: A private key held in your laptop's TPM chip
ambiguous.why: A bare private key is secret data, and some older material classes key material as 'something you know'. The phrase 'held in your laptop's TPM chip' is decisive here — the key is non-exportable and bound to a hardware token, so possession of the laptop is the factor. Marked as such, but a student who fixates on 'key = secret' can argue it.

ambiguous.item: A code generated by an authenticator app on your phone
ambiguous.why: The user types a code, which superficially looks like knowledge. It is 'something you have' because the code is only obtainable from the seed on the enrolled device. Standard answer, but this is the single most commonly mis-argued item in this set.

ambiguous.item: Separation of duties on payment approvals
ambiguous.alternative: OUT (technical, if enforced in the payment system)
ambiguous.why: Separation of duties is an administrative/managerial control in ISC2 material — it is a rule about how roles are assigned. It is frequently enforced technically inside an ERP or payments system, so a student who classes the enforcement mechanism rather than the control itself will argue technical. The control as written is administrative.

ambiguous.item: A badge-operated turnstile in the lobby
ambiguous.why: Badge systems are hybrid: the turnstile is a physical barrier but the badge reader and its access list are a technical/logical control. It is not administrative under any reading, so OUT is safe here — flagged only because students often want to split it.

assignment.You tell a client up front that a specia: Canon III — provide diligent and competent service to principals

ambiguous.item: You decline to exaggerate a threat in a sales pitch to frighten a prospect into buying
ambiguous.alternative: Canon IV — advance and protect the profession
ambiguous.why: Refusing to misrepresent is squarely Canon II honesty. But the ISC2 Canon IV guidance explicitly warns against 'sensationalism' and against misrepresenting the profession for commercial gain, so a student citing that line has a real argument. I key II because the actor's own honesty in a client-facing statement is the primary conduct.

ambiguous.item: A client pressures you to overstate their security posture in an audit report, and you refuse
ambiguous.alternative: Canon III — provide diligent and competent service to principals
ambiguous.why: The principal is the client, so 'service to principals' is in play. Canon II wins because the conflict is resolved by honesty and legality overriding what the principal wants — the canons are applied in order and II precedes III. A student who reads it as a duty-to-client item is not being unreasonable.

ambiguous.item: You report a peer who is selling leaked ISC2 exam questions to candidates
ambiguous.alternative: Canon II — act honourably, honestly, justly, responsibly and legally
ambiguous.why: Exam-integrity violations are the textbook Canon IV case (protecting the certification and therefore the profession). But reporting misconduct is also plain honest/just conduct under II. IV is the keyed answer because the harm is specifically to the credential.

ambiguous.item: You turn down a second client whose work would create a conflict of interest with your current engagement
ambiguous.alternative: Canon II — act honourably, honestly, justly, responsibly and legally
ambiguous.why: Canon III guidance names conflicts of interest directly ('avoid apparent or actual conflicts of interest'), so III is keyed. Some instructors file conflict-of-interest under acting 'justly' in Canon II. III is better supported by the published guidance.

ambiguous.item: To report a suspected phishing email, click Report, then forward it to the security inbox
ambiguous.why: It is an ordered set of steps for completing a task, so Procedure. A student might read the reporting obligation itself as policy-level. The sentence states the how, not the mandate, so Procedure holds.
